title: Artificial Intelligence: Use Cases in Life Insurance

questions.stem: In the context of artificial intelligence for insurance, machine learning is best described as:

opts.x: A system programmed with specific rules by insurance actuaries to calculate premiums automatically.
Algorithms that learn patterns from labelled historical data and use those patterns to make predictions on new cases.
Software that mimics human speech to conduct customer service conversations.
A type of advanced spreadsheet tool that can process insurance data faster than traditional databases.

questions.answer: (B) Algorithms that learn patterns from labelled historical data and use those patterns to make predictions on new cases.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Machine learning (ML) is the branch of artificial intelligence in which algorithms improve their performance by learning from data, without being explicitly programmed for each specific task. In a supervised learning context (the most common for insurance applications), the algorithm is trained on labelled historical data (e.g., past claims with outcomes labelled as 'fraudulent' or 'legitimate') and learns to identify the patterns that distinguish the two classes. It then applies those learned patterns to new cases (new claims) to make predictions.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes an expert system or rule-based system, in which a programmer explicitly codes the decision rules ('if BMI > 35 AND diabetic, load premium by 15%'). Rule-based systems do not learn from data; they execute programmed rules.
(C) describes Natural Language Processing (NLP) or a conversational AI system, a specific application of AI, not the general definition of machine learning.
(D) A spreadsheet tool is a calculation and data organisation tool, fundamentally different from an ML model that identifies patterns in data.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025 and NDPA 2023, when an AI model recommends declining a life insurance application, the insurer must:

opts.x: Accept the AI model's recommendation as final.
Automatically issue a standard-rated policy as an alternative.
Ensure a qualified human underwriter reviews and confirms the decline before communicating it to the applicant, and provide a human explanation of the decision.
Refer the application to NAICOM for independent review before issuing the decline.

questions.answer: (C) Ensure a qualified human underwriter reviews and confirms the decline before communicating it to the applicant, and provide a human explanation of the decision.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NDPA 2023 Section 35 gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects on them. A life insurance decline, which affects the applicant's access to financial protection, is a significant effect. The insurer must therefore ensure: (1) a qualified human underwriter reviews the AI's recommendation before the decline is communicated; and (2) the applicant receives a human-comprehensible explanation of the specific reasons for the decline (not merely 'the AI model declined your application'). NIIRA 2025's TCF framework reinforces this; the consumer must understand the decision that affects their rights.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Accepting the AI's recommendation as final violates NDPA 2023 Section 35's human oversight requirement for significant automated decisions.
(B) No regulatory provision requires an insurer to offer a standard-rated policy when a risk is genuinely not acceptable at any standard terms.
(D) NAICOM does not review individual underwriting decisions; the insurer must apply its own governed underwriting process.

questions.stem: A lapse propensity model in life insurance is primarily used to:

opts.x: Predict which claims are likely to be fraudulent before the claim is filed.
Identify policyholders at elevated risk of lapsing in the next 30–90 days, enabling targeted conservation intervention.
Calculate the surrender value payable to policyholders who request early policy termination.
Recommend premium increases for policies with a history of late payment.

questions.answer: (B) Identify policyholders at elevated risk of lapsing in the next 30–90 days, enabling targeted conservation intervention.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A lapse propensity model is a predictive analytics tool that processes policyholder data (payment history, engagement signals, demographic features, product type, agent status) to generate a probability score for each policyholder indicating their likelihood of lapsing in the near term. Policies identified as high-lapse-risk are then prioritised for proactive conservation outreach (a call from the conservation team, a WhatsApp reminder, or an agent visit) before the grace period expires. The model's commercial value is in enabling cost-efficient conservation: the team focuses its limited contact capacity on the 5–10% of policyholders most at risk, rather than contacting all 100%.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Fraud prediction models identify suspicious claim behaviour after a claim is filed, a different use case with different data inputs and output variables.
(C) Surrender value calculation is a deterministic actuarial calculation from the policy's benefit and reserve structure, not a prediction model.
(D) Premium increases are a product pricing and underwriting decision, not the output of a lapse propensity model.

questions.stem: The NDPA 2023's provision on automated decision-making (Section 35) is relevant to AI use in insurance because:

opts.x: It requires all insurance companies to use AI-powered underwriting for all new business applications.
It gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or significant effects, requiring human review of adverse automated decisions.
It prohibits the use of any AI or machine learning technology in the assessment of insurance claims.
It requires insurers to publish their AI model algorithms for public inspection on the NDPC website.

questions.answer: (B) It gives data subjects the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or significant effects, requiring human review of adverse automated decisions.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Section 35 of the NDPA 2023 is Nigeria's equivalent of GDPR Article 22; the automated decision-making provision. It does not prohibit automated decisions; it requires that where such decisions produce legal or similarly significant effects (insurance decline; significant premium loading; claim refusal), the data subject must have the right to obtain human review of the decision. The insurer cannot hide behind the AI model's output as a basis for refusing to explain or review an adverse decision. This provision is the most directly applicable NDPA requirement to AI use in insurance underwriting and claims.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Section 35 is a right of the data subject; it imposes a human oversight obligation. It does not require any particular technology to be used.
(C) Section 35 does not prohibit AI in claims assessment; it requires human review availability for significant automated decisions.
(D) Publishing algorithms is not required by Section 35; the right is to human review, not to algorithmic transparency.

questions.stem: An AI model that produces systematically lower credit scores or higher insurance loadings for applicants from a specific geographic area, where that area predominantly reflects a particular ethnic group, is an example of:

opts.x: Actuarially justified risk differentiation, as geographic location is a valid insurance risk factor.
Disparate impact, a fairness violation in which an AI model produces systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups without pure actuarial justification.
Enhanced underwriting, as location data improves the accuracy of mortality risk prediction.
A compliance requirement under NIIRA 2025's product approval process.

questions.answer: (B) Disparate impact, a fairness violation in which an AI model produces systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups without pure actuarial justification.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Disparate impact (also called indirect discrimination) occurs when a facially neutral criterion (geographic area) produces systematically different outcomes for different demographic groups, in this case, effectively discriminating based on ethnicity through the proxy of location. Even if geographic location has some actuarial validity as a mortality predictor, an AI model that produces ethnic-group-correlated adverse outcomes must be evaluated against the proportionality standard: is the geographic differentiation actuarially necessary and proportionate, or is the location variable primarily serving as an ethnic proxy? If the latter, the model violates both NIIRA 2025's non-discrimination provisions and NDPA 2023's fair processing obligations.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Geographic location can be an actuarially valid risk factor for specific mortality causes (e.g., flood risk in the Niger Delta). However, the presence of actuarial justification for some geographic differentiation does not validate a model that produces ethnic-group-correlated adverse outcomes across all risk categories.
(C) 'Enhanced underwriting' describes additional evidence-gathering, not a model that produces systematically discriminatory outcomes.
(D) A discriminatory model output is a regulatory violation, not a compliance requirement.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer wants to deploy an AI fraud detection model for its life insurance claims. The insurer has 8 years of claims data (45,000 total claims) but only 890 confirmed fraud cases, all identified through post-settlement SIU investigations. The data scientist proposes training a supervised learning fraud classifier on this data.
(a) Identify two specific data quality challenges this dataset presents for training a reliable fraud detection model.
(b) Explain the ‘false positive’ problem in this context and describe the operational consequence if the fraud model has a high false positive rate in a bereavement claims context.
(c) Describe the human oversight mechanism that must be in place before any claim is delayed or referred to the SIU based on the model’s output.
(d) Identify three NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines requirements for AI model governance that this fraud detection model must satisfy before deployment.

model.h: Part (a): Two Data Quality Challenges

Challenge 1: Severe class imbalance: With only 890 confirmed fraud cases out of 45,000 total claims (approximately 2% fraud rate), the dataset is severely imbalanced. Standard ML classifiers trained on imbalanced data tend to predict the majority class (legitimate claims) for nearly all cases, achieving 98% accuracy while correctly identifying almost no fraud. The model must be trained with class-balancing techniques (oversampling fraud cases using SMOTE; undersampling legitimate claims; or using class-weight adjustments) to produce a model that can actually identify fraud.

Challenge 2 (Survivorship bias in the fraud labels: All 890 confirmed fraud cases were identified through post-settlement SIU investigations) meaning they were initially paid before fraud was detected. This creates a systematically biased training dataset: the 'confirmed fraud' label is only available for fraudulent claims that were sophisticated enough to be initially paid (and then subsequently investigated). Fraudulent claims that were declined during the initial assessment process are not labelled as fraud in the dataset; they are labelled as 'declined claims' (potentially legitimate). The model therefore learns from a biased sample of fraud patterns, those sophisticated enough to pass initial assessment, and may miss simpler fraud patterns or misclassify declined legitimate claims.
Part (b): False Positive Problem

A false positive in this context is a claim that the fraud model flags as suspicious, triggering an SIU referral or a settlement delay, when the claim is in fact legitimate.

In a bereavement context (death claims, where a widow or bereaved parent is the claimant), the operational consequences of a high false positive rate are severe:

1. NIIRA 2025 breach: If the SIU referral delays settlement beyond the 60-day statutory deadline, the insurer is in breach regardless of whether the SIU ultimately confirms the claim is legitimate. A high false positive rate creates systematic NIIRA 2025 breach exposure.

2. Profound consumer harm: A bereaved family who has lost their primary breadwinner is in acute financial distress. Delaying their claim payment based on an erroneous fraud flag, while the SIU investigates and finds nothing, causes real financial and emotional harm. NIIRA 2025's TCF principle and NAICOM's consumer protection mandate are directly implicated.

3. NPS destruction: A bereaved claimant whose legitimate claim is subjected to a fraud investigation and delayed payment will become a Detractor (NPS 0–6) for life. Their negative experience will be shared widely in their community, creating the exact trust deficit dynamic that suppresses insurance penetration.

Mitigation: The fraud model's decision threshold must be calibrated to minimise false positives in the bereavement context, accepting a somewhat lower fraud detection rate in exchange for fewer legitimate claims being incorrectly flagged.
Part (c): Human Oversight Mechanism

Before any claim is delayed or referred to the SIU based on the model's output, the following human oversight mechanism must be in place:

1. Senior claims assessor review: Every claim flagged by the fraud model must be reviewed by a senior claims assessor (not the model's output alone) who evaluates: the specific features the model identified as suspicious; the context of the claim (bereavement, critical illness); and any available independent information (death certificate corroboration; beneficiary relationship confirmation). The assessor decides whether the model's flag justifies escalation; the model's output is advisory, not determinative.

2. Dual authorisation for SIU referral: Any claim referred to the SIU must require dual sign-off, the senior claims assessor and the Head of Claims, ensuring that a human judgement of reasonable suspicion (not mere algorithmic output) triggers the delay.

3. Communication to the claimant: If a claim is delayed due to additional investigation, the claimant must be notified within the 5-day acknowledgement window that the claim is being assessed, with an explanation that does not reveal the fraud investigation (to avoid tipping off potential fraudsters) but does confirm that the insurer is processing the claim.
Part (d): Three NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines Requirements

1. Model documentation and explainability: The model must be fully documented, including: the training dataset; the variables used; the model architecture; the validation methodology; and the decision logic (at a level that enables a human reviewer to understand why the model flagged a specific claim). NAICOM inspectors must be able to review this documentation on demand.

2. Model validation before deployment: An independent validation of the model (by a person not involved in building the model) must be completed before the model is used to make or inform any claims decisions. Validation must include: performance on a held-out test set; disparate impact testing (to verify the model does not disproportionately flag claims from specific geographic or demographic groups); and a false positive rate assessment specifically in the bereavement context.

3. Ongoing monitoring and reporting: After deployment, the insurer must monitor the model's performance monthly against actual SIU investigation outcomes, tracking the true positive rate (fraud correctly identified), false positive rate (legitimate claims flagged), and the model's contribution to settlement delays. A quarterly model performance report must be provided to the Board Risk Committee, and any material model performance deterioration must be reported to NAICOM as part of the insurer's Insurtech model governance obligations.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer’s marketing team has proposed using an ML product recommendation engine to show personalised insurance product suggestions on the insurer’s mobile app. The recommendation engine will be trained on policyholders’ demographic data, existing product holdings, browsing history on the app, and transaction data from their mobile money accounts (accessed through an API partnership with a mobile money operator).
(a) Identify the specific NDPA 2023 consent and lawful basis requirements the insurer must satisfy before using mobile money transaction data as a model input.
(b) Describe two fairness safeguards the insurer must apply to the recommendation engine to comply with NIIRA 2025’s Treating Customers Fairly obligation.
(c) Explain the suitability limitation of a product recommendation engine, why a high-confidence product recommendation is not equivalent to a suitability assessment.
(d) Describe the NAICOM model governance requirements that apply to this recommendation engine before it can be deployed in a consumer-facing digital channel.

model.h: Part (a): Consent and Lawful Basis for Mobile Money Transaction Data

Mobile money transaction data is personal financial data, a category requiring careful lawful basis analysis under NDPA 2023:

1. Lawful basis: The insurer cannot rely on legitimate interests alone for processing detailed mobile money transaction history for insurance marketing purposes. The most appropriate lawful basis is explicit consent; the mobile money platform user must specifically consent to their transaction data being shared with the insurer for insurance product recommendation purposes. This consent must be:
• Separate from the mobile money platform's general terms of service (consent buried in T&Cs is not valid under NDPA 2023)
• Specific to the insurance use case (not a general data sharing consent)
• Freely given (the user must not lose access to the mobile money service if they decline)
• Revocable at any time

2. Data transfer mechanism: The API partnership between the insurer and the mobile money operator must be governed by a Data Processing Agreement that clearly: identifies the insurer as the data controller for the insurance recommendation use; restricts the mobile money operator's role to data transmission only; and specifies the categories of transaction data transferred, the purpose, and the security standards.

3. Privacy notice update: The insurer's mobile app privacy notice must be updated to disclose: the use of mobile money transaction data; the source of that data; the recommendation engine's logic (at a high level); and the user's right to opt out of the personalisation feature.
Part (b): Two Fairness Safeguards Under TCF

1. Product appropriateness filter: A high recommendation confidence score from the ML model does not equal product suitability. The recommendation engine must be constrained by a product appropriateness filter, products must not be recommended to a customer for whom the product is clearly unsuitable regardless of the model's confidence. Example: a participating endowment should not be recommended as a high-priority product to a customer whose transaction history shows irregular income and multiple overdraft events, even if the model has identified demographic patterns that correlate with endowment purchases in similar segments.

2. Demographic fairness testing: The recommendation engine must be regularly tested to verify that it does not systematically recommend higher-premium, more complex, or less suitable products to specific demographic groups (lower-income users, older users, users from specific geographic areas) relative to comparable segments. Under TCF Outcome 4, the insurer must not exploit demographic information to recommend products that serve the insurer's revenue interests ahead of the customer's protection needs. Quarterly fairness audits of the recommendation output, comparing product types recommended across customer segments, are a required governance mechanism.
Part (c): Recommendation is Not a Suitability Assessment

A product recommendation engine and a suitability assessment are fundamentally different:

A recommendation engine: Identifies products that are statistically associated with customers who share similar demographic and behavioural profiles with the target customer. It predicts what a similar customer has purchased, not what this specific customer needs. A high confidence score means 'customers like you have bought this product'; it does not mean 'this product is appropriate for your specific financial situation, risk appetite, and life goals.'

A suitability assessment: Is a structured process in which a qualified adviser: gathers information about the specific customer's financial position, income, expenditure, dependants, existing coverage, risk tolerance, and investment horizon; conducts a financial needs analysis; and identifies the specific product that best meets this specific customer's specific needs.

The gap: A recommendation engine cannot ask 'do you have other life insurance?' or 'do you have an outstanding mortgage?' It works from available data proxies. A suitability assessment captures this information explicitly and uses professional judgement to interpret it.

Compliance implication: For products above a defined complexity or premium threshold (endowments, whole life, participating plans), the recommendation engine may identify an interested prospect, but the actual recommendation of a specific policy must be preceded by a documented suitability assessment conducted by a qualified individual. The recommendation engine is a demand-generation tool; it is not the suitability process.
Part (d): NAICOM Model Governance Requirements Before Deployment

1. Pre-deployment DPIA: A Data Protection Impact Assessment (required under NDPA 2023 for high-risk processing) must be completed and approved by the DPO before the recommendation engine is deployed in the consumer-facing channel. The DPIA must address: the data processed; the fairness risks; the safeguards implemented; and the residual risks accepted.

2. Model documentation package: Full technical documentation covering: the model's training data; the recommendation algorithm; the fairness testing methodology and results; the appropriateness filter logic; and the explainability mechanism (how the app will explain to the user why a specific product was recommended).

3. Board and NAICOM notification: The NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines require notification of material AI deployments in consumer-facing digital channels. The Board must approve the governance framework for the recommendation engine, including the fairness audit schedule, the model monitoring plan, and the escalation criteria for model performance failures.

4. User transparency: The app must disclose to users that product recommendations are algorithmically generated; provide a way to understand the basis for a recommendation; and enable opt-out from personalised recommendations without loss of access to the app's other features.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer’s Statutory Actuary is considering using an ML-based mortality prediction model to inform the annual actuarial investigation and the pricing assumptions for a new product. The model was built by an external data science firm using the insurer’s historical policy data.
(a) Describe the documentation requirements for the ML mortality model that the Statutory Actuary must have in place before relying on its outputs in the annual investigation.
(b) Explain why the Statutory Actuary cannot simply rely on the model’s performance metrics (accuracy, AUC score) as evidence of its suitability for a regulated actuarial function.
(c) Describe the model validation approach that must be completed by a person independent of the model development team.
(d) Explain how the Statutory Actuary must present the model’s contribution to the actuarial assumptions to the Board’s Risk Committee to satisfy NIIRA 2025’s governance requirements.

model.h: Part (a): Documentation Requirements

Before the Statutory Actuary can rely on the ML mortality model's outputs in the annual actuarial investigation, the following documentation must be in place and reviewed:

1. Model development documentation: Complete specification of the training dataset (years covered; policies included; exclusions; how mortality events were labelled); the model architecture (algorithm type; hyperparameters; feature selection rationale); the validation methodology used during development (train/test split; cross-validation approach); and performance metrics on the validation dataset.

2. Variable documentation: For each input variable used by the model: its actuarial justification (why this variable is expected to be predictive of mortality); its data source (is it from the insurer's own PAS? From a third-party data feed?); and any known data quality issues.

3. Limitations documentation: The model developer must document: the model's known limitations; conditions under which its predictions may be unreliable (edge cases; populations not well-represented in the training data); and the scenarios in which the actuary should override or supplement the model's output with traditional actuarial judgement.

4. Scope of use definition: A clear specification of what the model is and is not authorised to do, for example, 'the model provides a supplementary mortality risk score that informs the actuary's annual experience investigation; it does not replace the actuarial tables or the Statutory Actuary's professional judgement on pricing assumptions.'
Part (b): Why Performance Metrics Are Insufficient

Accuracy and AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) measure the model's predictive performance on the test dataset; they are necessary but not sufficient evidence of suitability for a regulated actuarial function:

1. The test dataset may not represent future conditions: An AUC of 0.85 on a test dataset drawn from 2016–2022 data tells the actuary that the model was good at predicting mortality in those years, in that insured population, under those economic and epidemiological conditions. It does not tell the actuary whether the model will be equally accurate for the current year's portfolio, which may differ in age distribution, product mix, and health composition, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic fundamentally altered mortality patterns.

2. Performance metrics do not reveal actuarial consistency: The model may produce a good AUC while generating mortality rates for specific age/gender/health combinations that are inconsistent with established actuarial knowledge. A model that predicts very low mortality for 65-year-old smokers (because the training data happened to include a very healthy group of 65-year-old smoking policyholders) has a fundamental actuarial error that performance metrics do not reveal.

3. Regulatory function requirements exceed predictive accuracy: The Statutory Actuary's annual investigation report must satisfy NIIRA 2025's prescribed standards, certifying that the mortality assumptions are appropriate for the in-force portfolio. This certification requires professional actuarial judgement that the mortality rates, adjusted by the ML model's insights, remain within the bounds of actuarially sound practice, a standard that cannot be reduced to a single performance metric.
Part (c): Independent Model Validation Approach

The independent validation must be conducted by a person (internal or external) who was not involved in building the model:

1. Data validation: Verify that the training dataset correctly represents the insurer's in-force policyholder population, checking that it includes all relevant products, all relevant vintage years, and has not systematically excluded populations that might have different mortality profiles.

2. Technical validation: Re-run the model training and validation using the documented methodology, confirming that the reported performance metrics are reproducible. Test the model on an additional out-of-time validation dataset (data from a period not used in training, such as the most recent 12 months) to assess whether performance holds on genuinely new data.

3. Actuarial validation: Compare the model's mortality predictions for key demographic and product segments against: the insurer's own historical experience investigation; the EFU Life Table mortality rates; and published studies on Nigerian insured life mortality. Flag any segments where the model's predictions are actuarially implausible.

4. Disparate impact validation: Test whether the model produces systematically higher or lower mortality predictions for specific geographic, gender, or occupational groups, particularly groups that may be underrepresented in the training data and therefore prone to unreliable predictions.

5. Validation report: The independent validator produces a written report with a conclusion on whether the model is suitable for use as an input to the annual actuarial investigation, and any conditions or limitations that must accompany its use.
Part (d): Board Risk Committee Presentation

The Statutory Actuary's presentation to the Board Risk Committee must:

1. Describe the model's role and scope: Explain clearly what the ML model does (supplements the mortality experience investigation with pattern recognition from 45,000+ policy records), what it does not do (replace actuarial tables or professional judgement), and the limitations on reliance.

2. Present the validation findings: Summarise the independent validation's conclusions, including any concerns raised and how they were addressed before the model was used in the investigation.

3. Quantify the model's contribution: Show the Board Risk Committee the specific mortality assumption adjustments informed by the model's outputs, and the counterfactual (what assumptions the actuary would have adopted using traditional methods alone). This enables the Committee to understand the model's actual impact on the reserving and pricing conclusions.

4. Confirm regulatory compliance: Confirm that: the model's use complies with NDPA 2023 data processing requirements; the model satisfies NAICOM's Insurtech Guidelines model documentation standards; and the Statutory Actuary's professional certification covers the use of the model as an actuarial tool (not just the model's output without professional judgement).

5. Propose the annual review schedule: The Board Risk Committee should formally approve the model governance framework, including the annual validation schedule, the trigger conditions for model withdrawal (e.g., if performance deteriorates significantly on an out-of-time test), and the named responsible person for model oversight.

questions.stem: AI has the potential to fundamentally transform the Nigerian life insurance industry: enabling accurate risk pricing for previously uninsurable populations using alternative data, eliminating fraudulent claims that currently drain industry profitability, and delivering personalised financial advice through AI-powered chatbots to customers who cannot afford a human financial adviser. However, AI also presents specific risks: discriminatory model outputs that systematically disadvantage certain customer groups, opaque decisions that policyholders cannot understand or contest, and the possibility that AI confidence in insurance decisions outpaces the quality of the underlying data. Critically evaluate the proposition that the transformative potential of AI in Nigerian life insurance outweighs its risks, and design a governance framework that would enable a Nigerian life insurer to realise the benefits while managing the risks responsibly.

model.h: Thesis

The transformative potential of AI for Nigerian life insurance is genuine, and for specific, well-defined use cases with adequate data, it already outweighs the risks. For other use cases (particularly those involving adverse decisions about individuals, or those that require data quality that Nigerian insurers do not yet possess) the risks currently outweigh the benefits. The question is not whether AI should be used in Nigerian life insurance but which AI, for which purposes, under which governance conditions, in which sequence.
AI Opportunities for Nigerian Life Insurance

1. Risk pricing for uninsurable populations: Traditional actuarial underwriting requires a medical examination and documented income, excluding Nigeria's 60%+ informal sector from individually underwritten life products. AI underwriting models trained on alternative data (mobile money patterns, digital transaction behaviour, geolocation of economic activity) can price mortality risk for previously uninsurable populations without medical examinations, expanding the addressable market by tens of millions of potential policyholders.

2. Fraud detection at claims scale: The Nigerian life insurance market estimates fraud losses at 5–15% of total claims cost, a significant drag on industry profitability and a driver of premium inflation. A well-designed fraud detection model can identify fraudulent claim patterns (document forgery, agent-coordinated claims, phantom member schemes) at a scale and speed that human SIU teams cannot match.

3. Conservation at scale: A lapse prediction model that identifies 10,000 at-risk policies per week enables the insurer to direct limited conservation resources to the highest-impact interventions, improving persistency by 5–10 percentage points at a CAC of ₦5,000–₦15,000 per policy conserved rather than ₦65,000 to replace each lapsed policy.

4. Personalised financial advice accessibility: An AI-powered financial advice chatbot (trained on the FNA methodology, tax planning frameworks, and product suitability criteria) can provide a basic financial needs analysis and product recommendation to consumers who cannot afford a human financial adviser. In a market where fewer than 1% of Nigerian adults have access to qualified financial planning advice, this is a genuine financial inclusion contribution.
Specific AI Risks

1. Discriminatory model outputs: AI models trained on historical insurance data perpetuate historical discrimination, if women, low-income groups, or northern Nigerians were historically underserved by Nigerian insurance, the training data reflects this under-service. Models trained on this data will reproduce the same exclusions. Disparate impact testing is not a compliance checkbox; it is the only mechanism that can detect systematic discrimination in a model whose internal logic may be opaque.

2. Opacity and explainability: Complex neural networks and ensemble models produce outputs that their creators cannot fully explain at the individual-case level. A policyholder whose claim is declined based on an XGBoost model's 200-feature ensemble analysis cannot meaningfully contest the decision if the insurer cannot explain which features drove the output. NDPA 2023 Section 35 requires explanations; some AI architectures cannot provide them.

3. Data quality misalignment: The AI model is only as good as the data on which it was trained. If the training data contains errors (incorrect mortality labels; systematically incomplete demographic records; biased fraud labels from post-settlement SIU detection), the model will learn those errors and embed them in its predictions. Nigerian life insurers' legacy PAS data quality challenges (Chapter 29) make this risk particularly acute.
Conditions Under Which Benefits Outweigh Risks

The benefits outweigh the risks when:
1. The use case involves data that the insurer genuinely possesses in clean, complete form (lapse prediction using the insurer's own policy and payment data, yes; mortality pricing using 3 years of claims data from 5,000 policies, no).
2. The AI model's output is advisory (supporting a human decision) rather than determinative (replacing a human decision) for adverse outcomes.
3. The model has been independently validated against the specific population and time period it will be applied to.
4. A fairness audit has confirmed that the model does not produce disparate impact against identifiable groups.
5. The governance framework (below) is in place and actively functioning.
Governance Framework Design

Tier 1: Model classification: All AI models used in insurance decisions are classified by risk level: High Risk (models that produce adverse decisions for individuals, underwriting decline; claim referral; conservation escalation); Medium Risk (models that inform but do not determine decisions, lapse propensity scoring; product recommendation); Low Risk (models with no individual adverse impact, aggregate market analytics; premium trend modelling). High Risk models require the most intensive governance.

Tier 2: Pre-deployment requirements (High Risk): Independent validation; DPIA; disparate impact testing; full documentation package; Board Risk Committee approval; DPO sign-off.

Tier 3: Operational governance: Human review requirement for all High Risk model outputs before adverse decisions are communicated; monthly false positive rate monitoring; quarterly fairness audit; model performance dashboard reviewed by the Risk Committee.

Tier 4 (Annual review and revalidation: Every High Risk model is revalidated annually against its most recent 12 months of operational data) confirming that its performance has not deteriorated and that it remains within the approved governance parameters.

Tier 5: NAICOM reporting: Material AI model deployments and any significant model performance failures (AUC decline >10%; identified disparate impact) are reported to NAICOM as part of the insurer's Insurtech model governance obligations.

questions.stem: ‘The fundamental constraint on AI in Nigerian life insurance is not technology; it is data. Nigerian life insurers have access to the same global AI platforms as any insurer in the world. What they do not have is the decades of clean, structured, consistently recorded policy data that makes those platforms work. Until Nigerian insurers invest seriously in data quality (in how they capture, record, and maintain policyholder and claims data in their PAS systems) AI will continue to promise more than it delivers for the Nigerian market.’ Critically evaluate this proposition, drawing on the specific data requirements for each AI use case described in Chapter 31.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is substantially correct and the most practically important observation about AI in the Nigerian insurance context. Global AI platforms are available to Nigerian insurers on the same terms as to insurers anywhere; the barrier is not access to TensorFlow, XGBoost, or Azure Machine Learning. The barrier is that effective AI requires clean, structured, labelled, and sufficiently large training data, and the state of Nigerian life insurers' policyholder data, claims records, and mortality experience data makes this the binding constraint.
Data Requirements by AI Use Case

Fraud detection: Requires a sufficient volume of confirmed fraud cases with accurate labels. As the Q6 worked example shows, 890 fraud cases from 45,000 total claims (2% prevalence) is a very small training set for a reliable fraud classifier. International experience suggests that fraud detection models require at minimum 3,000–5,000 confirmed fraud examples to produce statistically robust pattern recognition. Most Nigerian life insurers have far fewer, and those they have are subject to the survivorship bias noted in Q6.

Lapse prediction: This is the most data-ready AI use case for Nigerian life insurers, the required data (payment history, policy tenure, agent status, product type, contact history) is generated by the PAS for every in-force policy, every month. An insurer with 50,000+ policies and a modern PAS likely has sufficient data quality and volume for a lapse prediction model within 18–24 months of PAS modernisation.

Alternative data underwriting: Pricing mortality risk for the informal sector using mobile money transaction patterns requires: a large dataset of mobile money users who subsequently became life insurance policyholders; mortality outcomes for those policyholders; and the mobile money transaction data for the period before their death. No Nigerian life insurer currently has this complete dataset; it would require a multi-year partnership between a mobile money operator and a licensed insurer to build the training data from scratch.

Mortality experience modelling: Requires clean policy-level records linking each policy to its outcome (alive at end of year; died; lapsed; surrendered; matured). Legacy PAS systems that do not maintain complete, consistent, and continuously updated policy records, with all status changes timestamped and reconciled, cannot generate the training data required for actuarial-grade mortality modelling.
Specific Data Quality Problems in Nigerian Life Insurance

1. Incomplete PAS records: Legacy PAS systems frequently have incomplete records, missing fields, inconsistent coding of policy status changes, and data entry errors accumulated over years of manual processing. A mortality model trained on data with 15% missing values for a key variable (age, sum assured, health declaration responses) will embed those gaps in its predictions.

2. Inconsistent historical data: Many Nigerian life insurers have migrated between PAS platforms, each migration potentially creating data mapping errors, truncated historical records, and inconsistencies in how fields are populated. The resulting dataset is not a clean longitudinal record; it is a patchwork of inconsistent data from multiple systems.

3. Claims data incompleteness: Claims that were declined, paid ex gratia, or settled by negotiation without full documentation may not be accurately recorded in the PAS. A fraud detection model trained on claims data that systematically under-records settlement outcomes will have an unreliable label set.

4. Mortality outcome gaps: Because many Nigerian life policies lapse before the insured event occurs, and because death registration is incomplete in Nigeria (not all deaths are officially registered, particularly in rural areas), the mortality data available to a Nigerian life insurer may undercount actual deaths, creating a systematically biased training dataset for mortality models.
The Path Forward: Data Investment as AI Investment

The proposition's practical implication is that the most effective pre-condition for AI investment is data governance investment:

1. PAS modernisation (Chapter 29): A modern, API-enabled PAS with rigorous data validation at entry point is the most impactful AI enabler. It creates the clean, structured, continuously updated data that every AI use case requires.

2. Data dictionary and standardisation: Before an insurer can train any model on its historical data, the data must be understood, every field documented; every code explained; every inconsistency between legacy and current PAS identified and resolved.

3. Prospective data capture for AI training: Certain AI use cases require data that does not yet exist in the insurer's historical records (e.g., alternative data underwriting). The insurer must begin capturing this data now, with consent, so that in 24–36 months it will have a training dataset of sufficient size and quality.

4. Data quality KPIs: The insurer should track data quality metrics as part of its operational dashboard, missing field rates; data entry error rates; PAS reconciliation exception rates. Improving these metrics is not just an operational discipline; it is AI capability building.
